utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. And good morning, everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Meek -- Ms. Nikolic -- oh. Where was he? Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Meek is here. Ms. Nikolic, Ms. Condon. And I don't see Mr. Haynes either, unless he is behind the -- no. Okay. From the Prosecution, it's -- And Mr. Lazarevic. From the Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Before we bring this witness in, you will recall that we need to decide a motion that was filed last week by the Prosecution seeking leave to amend the 65 ter list, exhibit list, with two exhibits pertaining to this witness that we are hearing today. This was filed confidentially on 9th October. Do we need to go into private session, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody. Mr. President, I don't believe we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking because it's been filed confidentially, that's all. We've only had one response that we are aware of and that's from Madam Fauveau. Does any other Defence team wish to state anything in relation? Okay. So we are seized with this motion, by which the Prosecution is seeking leave to amend the 65 ter list so as to add two exhibits, namely a video footage of the DutchBat withdrawal on the 21st of September 1995 and further a document consisting of an UNPROFOR summary of a meeting held on the 19th September 1995. As I said, we've had one response, namely from the Miletic Defence team. They do not essentially oppose the addition of the two documents to the 65 ter list, but they have requested the Trial Chamber not to take into account the description of the document and its relevance for the case as given by the Prosecution in its motion. Things being what they are, and there being no opposition from any of the Defence teams we are hereby deciding to grant the motion and the Prosecution is therefore being authorised to add to their 65 ter list the two exhibits to which I referred earlier. At the same time, we wish to assure Madam Fauveau, on behalf of General Miletic, that the description given by the parties to exhibits in the 65 ter list is of course not definitive and that significance and weight are given to exhibits not on the basis of how they are described but on the basis of their content in the light of other relevant evidence. I hope that allays your concerns and having disposed of this, I wish to know if there are any preliminaries you would like to raise. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the Defence teams? Okay. Let's bring -- this witness doesn't enjoy any protective measures, does he?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your present, current rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've left the army so I'm now a civilian working for the Halo Trust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. So thank you for coming over to give testimony in this case. Before you start your testimony our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll do our utmost to conclude your testimony as soon as possible. I don't know if that will be possible today, but if it's not, it's not expected to last beyond tomorrow. Mr. Thayer will go first. He will then be followed

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please states your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Tom Dibb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm now 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where you were born and raised?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I was born and brought up in Zimbabwe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago the Halo Trust. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what kind of work you do?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The Halo Trust is now, I think it's the biggest demining organisation working in nine countries around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long have you worked with the Halo Trust?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Pretty much since I left the army, so since 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What do you do with the Halo Trust?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm now a senior operations officer in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long have you been based in Afghanistan?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I've been base there had since March this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please list some of the locations just briefly where you've worked in the course of your work with the Halo Trust?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Mozambique, Republic of Georgia, Chechnya, Kosovo, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and a brief attachment in south Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just very briefly, sir, on a day to day level, what do you with the Halo Trust?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The present job involves managing 2870 Afghan staff spread across from Kabul northwards up to the Amur River so it's coordinating, controlling and finding funding for that project.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Thayer speak into the microphone, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will do. I'm being instructed to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to review with you your military history briefly and please correct me if there's anything I've gotten wrong or left out. You joined the British army in 1991, graduated Sandhurst in 1992, the army sent to you its language school where you studied the Serbo-Croat language, and then you were posted as a Lieutenant to Gornji Vakuf from November of 1993 to approximately May of 1994 as an interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, other than interpret --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Other than interpret, sir, did you take on any other responsibilities while you were serving as a liaison -- as an interpreter, forgive me?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, the -- saying interpreter is probably giving me far too much credit for my language skills. It was a basic colloquial course that we did, and I began attached to a company level liaison team and after a month or so, the man leading that team got sick and didn't return so I took over that liaison role.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you liaise with one particular side or the other in the course of that work?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In Gornji Vakuf is split with sort of a Croat-Muslim, it's sort of a split Croat-Muslim village. I did deal with both sides but the way it worked I was predominantly dealing with the Bosnian Muslims. I think there was probably a deliberate policy to have -- I had a counterpart, he did more time on the Croat side, and I think that was deliberate so that the parties we talked to didn't think we would go straight from their headquarters off to the other one and pass on information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were injured in the spring of 1994 in a land-mine explosion that injured you and a colleague and killed an officer. Where did you go after your injury? Where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: A few days after the injury, I was flown back to the U.K. Thereafter, my battalion deployed to Northern Ireland where I went with them to I think November that year, and then there was a possibility of another job in the former Yugoslavia which I returned to in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And prior to doing that, in January of 1995, you completed a sort of a refresher course in the Serbo-Croat language at the army language school and then were posted to Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as I think as you've mentioned, you left the army sometime at the end of 1995 or formally sometime in early 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you began working immediately with the Halo Trust after your military service?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I began work with Halo in April, so a couple of months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you returned to Bosnia in 1995, what was your position and assignment, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It was basically I was based out of Bosnia-Herzegovina command in Sarajevo working from General Smith's office. The main role was liaison to the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when did you begin this assignment, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Very early April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Physically were you and General Smith co-located?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- he obviously had his own private office, but we were in the outer office in the same building, just outside his.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did that building have a particular name? Was it referred to by a particular name?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was General Smith's formal position or title at that point?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: He was commander UNPROFOR within Bosnia itself, so within the greater chain, I think General Janvier based out of Zagreb was the senior officer in theatre. General Smith was the senior officer within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And directly below General Smith, did he have a Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Chief of Staff was Brigadier General Nicolai with Colonel Coiffet as deputy Chief of Staff and Lieutenant Colonel Baxter as the military assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you just briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what your duties as a liaison officer were?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think the idea of the post was to create a line of communication from the residency or from Smith's office through to the Bosnian Serb side, particularly their higher command, and it was to have a line of communication that didn't involve formal letters written by the general passed on to General Mladic. Now, some of the work was extremely mundane, setting up meetings, arranging vehicle passes and the like. And communication to the Serb side became considerably more difficult after air strikes in May I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who were your counterparts on the Serb side and let's start with the -- on the military side?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: On the military side, we would speak to the people in Lukavica barracks and they are the two key players were -- the key player was a guy called Colonel Indic. Under him was someone called Major Brane and there was a lady whose name I've temporarily forgotten, so the general contact there was through Colonel Indic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about on the civilian side?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: On the civilian side we would go through Lukavica into Pale and when we did get the opportunity it was generally speaking to a man called Jovan Zamejica who I believe was one of Karadzic's aides.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there a liaison officer for the Muslim side when were you based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, Captain Bliss arrived slightly after me and covered liaison more with the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall captain Bliss's first name?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Emma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer and Mr. Dibb, if you could kindly slow down a little bit and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did General Smith have a military assistant during the time you served with him?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. His military assistant was a Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember Colonel Baxter's first name?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I believe it's Jim.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to July of 1995. Did you receive an assignment in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Srebrenica enclave to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. In July 1995, the deputy Chief of Staff Colonel Coiffet was sent to Tuzla to I think brief back directly to the HC command what the situation was, what the situation was in Tuzla, and Colonel Coiffet took me along to help him on the interpreting side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that arrived in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure we arrived on Bastille Day which is the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you've told me yesterday that you're not that great with dates, but how is it that you recall that it was Bastille Day?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I was obviously with a French colonel who wanted to make something of it that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you describe, please, for the Trial Chamber, what you saw when you arrived in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think two things stick in my mind from that, and again I'll make apologies now for it being 12 years ago and a slightly shaky memory on fine detail, one was complete chaos on the UN side of things, and I think before we went out to see the displaced people from Srebrenica, we first attended what was supposed to be a coordination meeting run by the UN. It was complete chaos. It started before it should have, had to restart at least twice, tempers were frayed, and there was clearly very little coordination and very little happening that appeared constructive at that stage. After that, I think it was after that, we went out to see where the refugees were being received. Again, as you can imagine, people in pitiful condition, completely drained physically and emotionally, packed together very tightly, as far as I recall very little in the way of facilities for them at that early stage. Colonel Coiffet I remember addressed them, stood up on a vehicle, gave a speech, the details of which I don't particularly remember. I talked a little bit to some of the people who had come out, and again I don't remember details of what was said apart from again people were completely drained, there was comment on yes we are here but we don't have our men folk with us. I do remember being struck by the fact that there were only women and I think elderly men, young children, but no sort of teenage and above men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, was part of your assignment to find out what happened to the men of military age from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not that I recall. I think it was more to just get an understanding of what the situation was. I can't remember what sort of briefing General Smith was receiving but judging from the fact that there was such chaos on the UN side, I imagine he wasn't getting much coherent and hence Colonel Coiffet had been sent to try and pass back a clearer picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to the topic of the fate of the military-age men from Srebrenica, do you recall what your state of knowledge was on that 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not particularly. Certainly, what I can say is that at that stage we had no idea that anything untoward, as far as a massacre in Srebrenica, had occurred. That particular information we only received later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how long did you spend in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I would guess two or three days. We arrived on the 14th, one day obviously not the 14th, we drove down to Kladanj where people were being received too. So those are the two places that I recall and thereafter we returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during your time on this assignment did you see any groups of military-aged men arriving?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now later on in July, sir, did you receive another assignment to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. A few days after that, the Chief of Staff, Brigadier General Nicolai, deployed to Srebrenica to witness the Dutch troops leaving the enclave, and I was again asked if I could accompany him on that trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as briefly as you can, sir, can you describe what you did and what you saw on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: We deployed, I remember shortly before arriving at the town of Bratunac, a couple of guys came sort of charging out of the side of the road and stopped our vehicles. I recognised one of the guys who had stopped us as one of General Mladic's body guards who I had met on previous occasions. I jumped out of the vehicle and spoke to this man, explained who we were and what we were doing. He -- sort of mood changed completely, very cordial, he took me off to the right of the road, and a short distance off the road General Mladic was addressing a group of perhaps 50 of his troops and he said to us, "I just need to finish speaking to my guys. Please can you wait and I'll be with you." Once he had completed briefing his troops, he then did come out and escorted General Nicolai and the party to Bratunac where we sat with him in a room, and I believe we had a breakfast, brunch, with him. I don't particularly remember what we discussed at the time, but I remember Mladic was in very good form, he was full of bonhomie which obviously afterwards struck me as slightly disconcerting that he could be so full of steam and goodwill bearing in mind what we subsequently found out had occurred. Having left -- having finished that meal, we left Bratunac and went down to the bridge where the troops were, the Dutch troops, were leaving. I have a clear recollection of General Mladic standing there and saluting the Dutch vehicles as they left and turned off down the bridge. I think it was after the vehicles had left, Mladic then took us through past the Dutch Battalion headquarters. I recall the road there strewn with debris from where there had clearly been thousands of people camped outside the Dutch Battalion, bits of clothing, bits of blanket, filth everywhere, thoroughly unpleasant. Mladic then walked us through the village. I wouldn't say we went through the entire village. I remember being taken through a graveyard where he pointed out some damage to tombstones and I don't remember whether it was broken stones or stones with bullet scars on them, but there was talk of look what the Muslims have done, there is complete disrespect for our dead. We then were shown through a few of the buildings, and I believe after that we returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, a few days after that, did you receive another assignment to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime after that, again, I don't remember the date apart from that which is written in the statement, I was woken up in the dead of night and told a small delegation or a small group from the residency would be heading to Zepa to witness, monitor, the evacuation of civilians from that enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were woken up and given this assignment, were you told you would be going alone or with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I was going to be part of a two-people from the joint commission observers, JCOs were going, and I was to be attached to that team. I can't remember whether I was informed then or found out subsequently that UN civil affairs were also accompanying us to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just used the term "joint commission observers," sir. What is that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The JCOs were British Special Forces, soldiers, who were I think deployed across Bosnia. Very much in a liaison role, certainly a lot of the work that they were doing involved fairly similar liaison to what we were doing. Their advantage was I think probably the command felt they could stick them into fairly isolated parts of the country, knowing that they could, one, look after themselves, and, B, had good communications equipment back to headquarters location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the names of these two JCO officers off the top of your head?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I remember first names, not surnames, I believe it was Robert, captain, and Chris, a staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did I show you a document yesterday that jogged your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: You did, and I think the staff Sergeant might have been Craythorn surname, I don't remember the captain's surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we may have P02575 on e-court, briefly? Sir, you should is shortly have a document in front of you on your computer screen. It will be in English, I hope.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, it's on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the date of this document is the 20th of July, and as you can see it refers to the travel to Potocari on the 21st with General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a reference to a Captain Stevenson and a Sergeant Craythorn, who did not make that trip; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I believe that's correct. I certainly don't recall them being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. But what I believe what you told me yesterday was that this triggered your recollection about these guys being with you in Zepa, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yup, I'm pretty sure Craythorn definitely rings a bell, Stevenson, to be honest I'm not sure whether it was Rob Stevenson or Rob somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And the Captain Dibb referred there is yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did this document also jog your recollection as to when the actual date was that you were at the bridge in Bratunac, that being the 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's difficult to say it jogged my memory because I simply at that stage working seven days a week, everything was -- it was pretty hard to remember what day let alone what date. I've no reason to doubt the date shown on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to the second page of the English translation. And it's a one-page document in the original. Do you see the signatory there, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, prior to that trip that you took to Bratunac, had you ever heard of a General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm not sure. It certainly wasn't a name that I would have associated with a particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Did I -- do you recall me showing you a document yesterday about a meeting in September of 1995 attended by General Smith, yourself, General Dragomir Milosevic, and General Miletic in Sarajevo? Do you remember seeing that document?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you sit here today, do you have any specific recollection at all about that meeting or about General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I remember the meeting occurring, and I believe there was probably another one a couple of days later, discussing compliance with the cease-fire obligations imposed upon the Bosnian Serbs. Beyond that very general recollection of what was at the meeting, I simply don't recall relationships between people and what specifics were talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are done with that document. Thank you. Now, back to this early morning wake-up and this assignment with the two JCOs, what was the assignment, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: We were tasked to go to Zepa with communications equipment and report back to BH command to ensure that they were aware of what was happening on the ground in Zepa. Now, I'm not sure if this is my supposition afterwards or if it was briefing at the time, but I think we were all very clear that the aim of it was to try and ensure that things went differently there from how they had gone in Srebrenica a short while previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you make that reference, sir, to Srebrenica, what do you recall was the information, if any, that you had at that time in July about what had happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm fairly sure by that stage we had information that a massacre of some sort had occurred. I'm not sure if we realised quite the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to whom at BH command was your team to report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In the communications, the far end of our set was in the JCO office which was literally just across the way from down a flight of steps and into a container opposite General Smith's outer office, so we would have briefed JCOs to Colonel Baxter and from Colonel Baxter back to General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you referred to learning perhaps subsequently or soon thereafter that you were also to be accompanied by some civil affairs officers. Do you recall how many and do you recall any of their names?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: We had two. It was Ed Joseph and Viktor Bezrouchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And other than those two men, was anyone else tasked to go with you to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. We met up with -- and I can't remember at what stage -- a French colonel, I think his name might have been Jermaine, he was a 6 legionnaire, plus his interpreter who was way better at speaking the language than I was. I think we also met up with a Ukrainian captain who was also a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that Ukrainian captain, to your knowledge, sir, was based where?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think he was based out of Tito barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you referred to a French colonel who may have been a legionnaire. Can you just spell the name, as you recall it, for the record? I don't think it came out.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think J-E-R-M-A-I-N-E.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So did you all leave together at the same time or how did that -- how did that departure go, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again I'm slightly sketchy on my memory of that. I would guess we did but I can't guarantee it. We certainly ended up together at OP 2 at the top of the hill in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you describe that location just generally and briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: As I recall it, it was sort of a following down a reasonable dirt road through a wooded area. I think it was more sort of fir trees. On the crest of a hill with -- as you went through the location, then the road zigzagged down into the village of Zepa itself. I think there was a bit of barbed wire fencing and a barrier in the location as which would make sense, it being a check-point too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I want to you describe for the Trial Chamber what you saw when you got there, and let's start with any VRS officers and commanders?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, details sketchy but generals, General Mladic and General Tolimir, I recall both were there at the time. I recall that the ICRC and I think it was from their Pale office were also up at the top of the hill at that stage. We, I think, they were all sort of sitting on a fairly tight S bend on the road where there was a view down into the village. I think that's where we were standing at the time. The ICRC and our group were trying to get permission to go down into the village itself to see what it was happening essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to General Tolimir. Had you met him prior to this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When and in what context?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, part of the liaison role from BH command, we would -- if Smith was trying to have a top level meeting, Mladic was a man he'd try and get to, but often it was slightly easier to get hold of Tolimir, and certainly, if it wasn't going to be General Smith personally present, we had -- we would have a much better chance of seeing General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just referred to ICRC, and I believe yourself trying to get permission to enter town. From whom were you speaking permission, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: From General Mladic, as the senior officer on site, and I would say at that stage, we were all very much of the opinion that General Mladic was in control of what was happening in Zepa at that particular stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I managed to speak to Mladic and asked could I go down with the -- I can't remember why the JCOs didn't come down with us, but I arranged to go down in the same vehicle as the French colonel and his interpreter, so I went down with them. I believe ICRC and civil affairs came down I think at the same time. They were all certainly there shortly thereafter. I remember them both groups being in the village of Zepa sort of mid-day or maybe early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without revealing any identities, if you even remember them, of the ICRC personnel, do you recall how many there were there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think there was just a -- certainly I recall a single woman being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what if anything did you see on your way down into town?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Driving down the road, lots of VRS troops, sort of lining the road in a state of exhaustion which I guess is to be expected having spent a few days fighting. There were, I remember, lots of old money drifting about, slightly peculiar. There was a tank with some empty ammunition next to it on the road facing down into the valley. And as we got down to the bottom of the road, there were two, I recall, slightly new-looking log cabins, for want of a different word, with a barrier of some sort, which -- possibly a chain across the road, I don't remember exactly, and that appeared to be the limit that the VRS troops were being allowed into the village. So once we were passed that particular barrier, there were no more VRS troops in the village itself. We drove through the village, past the main square with a mosque and on to the Ukrainian company headquarters building, which I believe was located at pretty much the end of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop you right there and follow up on a couple of things. On the way into town, other than the tank, did you see any other weaponry or artillery?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In my statement I say I saw a couple of mortars. I'm afraid I don't actually remember that now. I have no reason to doubt my statement on that but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you describe that you reached a point where it appeared to you beyond which the VRS soldiers were not allowed. Not allowed by whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I would say not allowed by the VRS themselves, so through senior command ultimately General Mladic, but it's possible that decision was taken at a lower level. I'm simply not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you mentioned a couple of buildings or the main square and the mosque in the centre of town. Can you describe the buildings that you did see, can you describe their condition?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, not a clear memory particularly. I remember the square itself. It was open. It had a water fountain in it which subsequently was of great use in that it was a source of water for the displaced people coming in. The mosque single minaret and some of the houses had signs of shelling on them. Again the -- I don't have a clear distinct memory of individual buildings. It was houses where shell damage was very common across Bosnia at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And could you tell, sir, at that time, whether that evidence of shelling was recent or whether it was older?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. It was -- I was fairly confident that it was recent. It's pretty easy to tell, and if something has landed in a field it's easier to tell that the ground has been turned up in the last day or so rather than a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And other than the evidence of fresh shelling on some of the houses, did you actually see evidence of recent shelling on the roads or on the ground, as you just described it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. There were sort of shell craters. I'm fairly sure there was also what looked like a mine crater further up the road, with a disabled vehicle which was obviously of a concern to us driving down the road and into the village thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you were making your way towards the Ukrainian base in town. What did you do when you got there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Made our way to the base, stopped. As I recall there was a group of civilians from the village or the surroundings who were gathered outside. At that stage, it was a dribble of people and perhaps some 50, 80 civilians gathered there. There was a civilian doctor with the people. The Bosnian commander, Avdo Palic, was there. I remember a youth who was clearly mentally disturbed. And I think throughout the time, I don't remember seeing any men from teenage up to sort of, I don't know, 50s anyway. I do remember some old men, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall Colonel Palic saying anything at that time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. While we were down there, he gave a formal speech of sorts to us, in which he said, you know, these are the circumstances we find Zepa has fallen, and we hope that we will be treated in a humane manner by which I certainly understood that to mean we don't want the same to happen here as happened to the menfolk in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You referred to a local doctor. First of all, do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it was Dr. Benjamin, or Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was he doing, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: To some extent, he appeared to be the -- for want of a better word again, senior civilian within the -- within the group of people who were there, and the point of contact as it were representing the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what if anything did he appear to actually be doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In addition to curing the civilian people that we also had some injured men in the village, and fairly obviously as a doctor he was concerned that these guys would get evacuated out -- out of the enclave and get decent medical attention. So that was occupying his attention to some extent and was asking our delegation what we could do to assist with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have any contact with the ICRC representative during this time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. I remember being particularly frustrated with the ICRC attitude, and I hasten to say it's an organisation I've in the sense got the highest regard for. This is one of the few occasions where I've -- I have been frustrated with them. We -- it was obvious that the population were going to get shifted out or would move out of Zepa, and discussions amongst ourselves were what we should be doing, there is very little that we can do, but one of the very few things that we could do is list everybody as they get on to the vehicles; and therefore, hopefully we can check that list at the far end to make sure that everyone who got on also got off. I for one was expecting that the ICRC would be involved in that process, but they flatly refused and I'm pretty certain the wording was, you know, we can't do that as we'll be seen to be participating in ethnic cleansing. And it just seemed to me to be avoiding the issue and things were going to happen, there was something we could do to make it better, why not do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any VRS officers in town during this time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. General Tolimir himself came down at some stage. I can't remember if he was there from the start or if he came in slightly later. But it was through General Tolimir that we got permission to move out the injured personnel, and I believe they moved in Ukrainian APCs. I've been sort of thinking about why an APC is, and I'm guessing it's because they were men of fighting age, men who had actually participated in the fighting, and therefore we felt they needed a protected vehicle to get them out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall who went with these wounded men?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think they were driven out by, as I say Ukrainian vehicles, Ukrainian drivers, but Dr. Benjamin, Benjamin accompanied them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you go next, sir, after these wounded were moved out?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Once they had gone, we then went back up to the top of the hill again, to OP 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you went back up to OP 2, approximately what time of the day was this, just to give us a rough idea?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'd hazard a guess at 3.00 in the afternoon but it is a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. When you returned to that elevation, were you able to see anything that you recall today down in the valley?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. It was apparent at that stage that things were starting to be set on fire, you could -- there is a view out and sort of haystacks and buildings, not within the tight village confines itself but sort of drifting up the flanks of the valley, haystacks and buildings were being set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What kind of buildings, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'd say probably residences, but you know some would be farm buildings, some would be buildings that people lived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you return back down into town later that day?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And when we went back down, the JCO Land Rover that I had come in with the JCOs accompanied us to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What did you do when you returned to town?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I believe that same afternoon, by now probably evening, the first buses and trucks were sent down into the village from the -- where they had been waiting up at the top of the hill, and we managed to load in, I guess, probably 20 vehicles worth of people from the square got into the -- got into the vehicles and left the enclave being taken through to Kladanj. It's -- what I do recall is when we came back down the hill again the number of people within the village had increased significantly. A lot had come in. Whether the earlier evacuation of the wounded had triggered something on the confidence scale, perhaps it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the age and gender composition of this group of civilians that you saw upon your return to town that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Female on the whole, plus young children.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were there any men?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: There were, some -- definitely some old men, and I remember on -- clearly not on this particular day, but on the last day I do remember escorting from his house to the square a particularly old guy who clearly didn't have any real understanding of what was happening apart from that he was being moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this time you were in Zepa among the civilians, did you speak with any of them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from speaking with them and observing them, can you describe their emotional state?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, to some extent drained. They wanted to leave Zepa at that stage without question. And a couple of -- a couple of instances, they -- towards the -- towards the end of the evacuation, we'll call it that, a -- it looked as though the last truck of the day had come but then another vehicle arrived, and there was a mad rush of people to get on to that which was a clear indication people wanted to leave. It's -- I've been thinking about it in the last sort of 24 hours, particularly, again, I'm just trying to think what is -- what was different about -- about this from, since then I've seen Grozny December 1999, I'd been in south Lebanon last year. And I think what strikes me as different between Zepa and those two is that in the first two the people, war always displaces people, and I think they try to leave at what they judge is the last safe moment to get out. Now, in Grozny and south Lebanon, the last safe moment was before the place was actually captures. They were leaving because loads of ordnance was piling into -- piling into their villages or into the town; whereas, here what was different is that the last safe moment to the population appeared to be the moment that the fighting had actually stopped, and the VRS were to some extent poised to enter the village or surrounding the village so they were scared. I've got no doubt of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell from speaking with the civilians, whether they had received any information about what had happened to the military-aged men of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm fairly sure they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what types of vehicles were used to move out the civilians when you returned there that day?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: As far as I recall, they were all civilian vehicles and a combination of buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know who supplied them and who drove them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The vehicles had been arranged by the VRS. I don't remember specifically who the drivers were but my guess is that they would have been civilian drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you spend that first night that you had -- after you had arrived in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: We spent the first night at the bottom of the hill at the Ukrainian compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do the next day, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The next day was going to be more of the same in that there were more people in the village, and quite a lot more had come in overnight, and the aim was to, together with the Serb command, to evacuate as many civilians as we could from the village. I recall on that day there was a slight panic amongst the people. There was another, I think some more injured people must have been leaving, and as before they were going to move out in armoured personnel carriers. When the population saw the armoured personnel carriers leaving, there was a feeling amongst the civilians that this was actually the UN evacuating the village themselves. So pretty much en masse they sat down on the road and blocked the exit from Zepa so nobody was going anywhere. I spent quite a bit of time myself talking to the people and convincing them that this wasn't the case, that what -- what simply what was happening was that another group of injured were moving, tried to give guarantees that we, the UN, were going to remain in the village. And while that story was being passed out and people gradually trusting us on that we, simultaneously spoke to, I think it was General Mladic again at the top of the hill, and said just to help things along could you send another group of, another packet of vehicles down for us, to show the civilian population this wasn't the last evacuation for them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, other than Dr. Benjamin on the first day, do any other local civilians stand out in your memory during the course of these transportations?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, they do and it's -- I mean, one particularly, I probably should have mentioned earlier, was the guy I called the hodza, who somehow associated with the mosque in Zepa. Youngish guy, clearly in no way a fighting man, but he was assisting with trying to put together lists of people leaving. Also to some extent being someone else we could speak to. He could then speak to the -- speak to the population in the absence of Dr. Benjamin earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again, understanding that your recollection of specific dates after 12 years isn't perfect, just can you describe or can you recall for the Court approximately how many days these transportations took?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. And again, as I mentioned to you yesterday, I had a bit of a problem even shortly afterwards trying to fit all the days into each other. But I think we got the first group out on the very first day that we arrived. I then think there were two full days of evacuations when the great majority of people left. At the end of that, there were still a group of about 400 people left who hadn't been moved. So they had to be moved out again as a fourth packet on what in my mind is the fourth day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where did you spend your nights during this process?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: As before, down at the bottom in based out of the Ukrainian camp. The first night we got offered -- the colonel was going to throw somebody out of his bed and offer us that which none of us wanted, so we slept out on the veranda. At some stage either that first night or the next morning we found one of the Ukrainian troops trying to pilfer our Land Rover. Thereafter, one of us -- we took turns, one of us would sleep in the vehicle every night and the other two outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. This was down in town, though; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: This was in town, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you estimate for the Trial Chamber approximately how many people arrived during the course of the two full days, as you've described them, of transportations, who were eventually moved out on those two days?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'd say close to 4.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described a group of about 400 people that remained on the second full day of the transportations --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- what did you do with respect to those people?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think as I mentioned they were pretty nervous, they thought that they had missed the boat essentially and were going to be abandoned in the village. They -- I think fairly reasonable psychological stress on them having seen everyone else leaving, not very sure what was happen, so they were in a -- slightly panicky, so we said listen, what we'll do is we'll put you all in a garden around the mosque, and we greed to deploy some French troops around them. And my recollection of that is that it was, it was not because we thought anything was going to happen to them, it was purely to reassure them that they hadn't been abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you referred to some French troops. Who were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think it was probably a company strength had come down under command of a French engineer colonel, and I'm trying again to think what triggered the sending of them. I certainly recall that I and the two JCOs were pretty unimpressed with the Ukrainian setup. They -- beautiful valley which probably had been pretty sleepy for the last couple of years, but clearly it had fallen into disrepair, sandbag walls were collapsed, troops didn't appear to have a full complement of boots. There weren't that many weapons. And I don't remember doing it, but I'm certain we must have reported back to BH command to say, listen these guys really aren't up to much down here, and I think that would have been well understood in that -- at command level. I'm pretty sure we all had slightly more faith in NATO forces than other people supporting the UN mission in -- in Bosnia at the time. So the French had been sent just to bolster the security generally in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when they did arrive, these -- this French contingent, commanded by this engineer colonel which you described, did you observe any interaction between that colonel and any VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In the course of this day, the Colonel Jermaine who had come in earlier, left, and things were handed over to command of the engineer colonel. It was in a very stark difference in command style between the two men. And I think the, I may be doing the man an injustice, but I would say he was bullied to some extent by the Serbs, certainly didn't stand up to them as Colonel Jermaine sort of appeared to in the early days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about General Tolimir arriving in town on the first day that you were there to authorise the movement of the wounded. Did you see him down in town again during the course of these days of the transportations?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. He was around -- he was around a few times. I know, on -- at the end of the first main day of movement, we spoke to him again there was a shall we shan't we send more troops -- send more troops, more vehicles that night, and the decision was no, let's leave it to tomorrow morning. I also remember seeing him on what in my recollection is the fourth -- the fourth morning, the day that we moved out the last 400 people. I recall him sitting with a bottle of alcohol down at the -- at what I described as the new-looking log cabins. So he was definitely down then, I would say slightly under the influence of alcohol that morning. We -- we were again debating the movement of another group of injured men and I'm afraid I don't remember at what stage these guys had arrived in Zepa. And at some stage on that morning, General Tolimir agreed that the guys could leave. Which they did. I note in my earlier statement I said I heard they had been pulled out of the vehicles at Rogatica. I'm afraid I simply don't remember now who told that to me. On that same day, I remember the hodza, who we mentioned earlier, was with the very last lot of people to be leaving Zepa, and I think probably at the top rather than at the bottom, as the vehicles were about to move, General Tolimir identified this guy and said, "Sorry, he is a man of military age. He therefore cannot be evacuated along with the women and children." The UN civil affairs team remonstrated but were overruled on that particular issue. By that stage, I'm fairly certain General Smith had left, and I don't think we contacted higher command on the issue. The hodza was taken away, certainly wasn't allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just referred to General Smith, sir. During these transportations, did you see him in town at all?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: My recollection is that he never made it beyond OP 2 at the top of the hill and didn't actually come into the village or town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know whether he was staying in the area overnight during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No. I'm pretty certain he would have been doing day trips which bearing in mind distances and timings involved would have given him some hours on each occasion at OP 2, but overnighting back in Sarajevo to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after the civilian population was moved out, what did you see happening in town next?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: On my day 4, we went up to the top of the hill, witnessed the hodza being taken off. We then went back down into town again that night. And it was -- it was clear then last of the civilians had moved and there had been the Serb troops were now allowed into the village itself, and without much delay, it was clear that houses were being looted, furniture, electrical appliances, whatever, were being bundled out, stuck into vehicles and driven up into the hills. Fairly early on I remember houses within the village itself being set alight, and this proceeded pretty much for the duration of the rest of the time that we remained in the Zepa area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to houses being set on fire, sir, who was setting them on fire?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I didn't actually watch anybody doing it, but it was in a very apparent cause and effect soldiers had moved into town, houses start going up on fire, so in my mind, anyway, I'm crystal clear that it was the VRS soldiers in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by this time, sir, to your knowledge, were there any Muslim civilians left in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No. And again, I'm pretty certain there weren't. We'd -- we'd had the hodza with us until the end who clearly knew his parish, shall we call it, pretty well, was talking to people. We'd also spoken to the Ukrainians and asked that they send their vehicles out to reconnoitre some of the outlying houses and hamlets to ensure that no one was left. We ourselves did a certain amount of checking houses within the village which is where we found that one old man I mentioned earlier, but I'm confident that there were Bosnian civilians or Muslim civilians left in Zepa at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, back to the -- this looting and the destruction of the property, did anyone in particular appear to be in charge of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: On to that first night, not particularly, but as the days went on, there was a -- I think he was a colonel, it maybe a Major Kusic from Rogatica brigade who was very much in evidence throughout, and I think by that stage, Mladic and Tolimir had gone and Kusic very much appeared to be the man in charge, and was up and down himself in his own red vehicle regularly. And again if we -- if we go back slightly to the earlier stage where somebody in the command structure had said you guys simply won't enter the village, clearly someone had now said you guys can enter the village, and again in my mind, the VRS were very professional officers, I'm absolutely certain if someone had said you can't do that, it wouldn't have been done. So whether it was an actual order or whether it was just a blind eye, I can't say, but it was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is an objection I'd like to raise. We are speculating. The witness thinks and the witness is supposing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Thayer. Do you wish to comments on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm reluctant to respond in the presence of the witness, but I'll try to be as generic as possible. I think he was referring to his experience observing the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I think if we draw the attention of the witness that in the course of his testimony, he needs to concentrate on facts and that you are aware of that you believe did happen, but avoid speculating on anything you're not sure about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think we can continue along those lines. We are in a position to know whether he's speculated or not in any way -- in any case. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I think the question itself was somewhat confusing. Mr. Dibb, do you think or do you know that whether Mr. Kusic was in charge of the looting and destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say he was the senior officer on the ground. He was participating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether he's responsible for the -- no, no. He was in charge of the looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I don't want to get myself in -- in difficulties on supposition and avoiding the question, but where I'm coming from on this is we are dealing with a military command structure and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what a you're saying he's in charge of the VRS there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's in charge of the VRS and participated in the looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kusic participated in the looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you describe it, Mr. Kusic participating in the looting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. It was -- I mean a series of vehicles going up and down the hill from OP 2 into the village of Zepa itself, with Mr. Kusic himself going up and down accompanying the vehicles that were coming back up laden with cattle, furniture and whatever else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, had you met this Kusic prior to your time there in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'd seen him before at Rogatica check-point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know to which brigade he was attached?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think he was Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this time when you saw Kusic during this looting, did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I remember clearly having an argument with him. He was very keen that we, the UN contingent, left, and at some stage I remember him proffering his watch and telling me that General Mladic had personally given him the watch in appreciation for whatever he'd done, and leading on from that conversation was General Mladic says, you guys have to leave, to which I said well, that's very interesting but General Mladic isn't my boss. My boss is General Smith. He was telling me that I have to stay so that's tough luck to you, Mr. Kusic. So it was a -- I actually probably enjoyed the exchange. He -- he was clearly annoyed at our presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point, sir, did this looting and burning appear to stop?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: As I recall, no, it went on throughout. I think they had sort of dealt with what was in the village itself and then started moving on to places slightly further afield, but again, as I say, as I recall now, it was still going on up until the point we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point did your freedom of movement change?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. We had -- as described, we had been based at the bottom of the hill in the village itself and had been able to get about, look into some of the houses to make sure that the population had indeed left. Once we had satisfied ourselves that the population had left, and the VRS were allowed back into the village, at that stage we were then largely restricted to -- sorry, staying in our vehicles and, well not staying in our vehicles, staying around the Ukrainian company headquarters and our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, while you were there in Zepa, did you become aware at any time that something had happened with respect to Colonel Palic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. At some stage we'd -- we'd seen him up at the top of the hill with, I think it was Colonel Furtula from Gorazde Brigade and at that stage the conversation was definitely heading in the direction of colonel -- sorry, Mr. Palic was not going to be allowed back down into the village. Furtula said in the course of conversation at that stage that no need to worry about him. I've worked with him before. I think in the army. My notes make reference to the TO which I simply have no idea what the TO might have been. But I believe they had been colleagues in the Yugoslav army before, and he said don't yeah, don't worry about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Had you met this Colonel Furtula before?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I had been into Zepa -- into sorry, Gorazde before so, yeah, I believe I had met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall there being any protest at any time about the treatment of Colonel Palic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Right now, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You referred to the seizure of the hodza. Do you recall precisely to whom you protested about that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The protest was to General Tolimir, as he was certainly there, and my recollection is that it was Tolimir who said this guy is of military age and can't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you referred a couple of times to the mosque that you saw there in the centre of town. Do you know what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I've never been back to Zepa again so I've -- I don't know for sure. However, I did meet the Ukrainian captain who told me that shortly after our group had left OP 2, the mosque was blown up. I subsequently raised that issue with Colonel Indic in Lukavica. He came back with a flippant reply that yes it was destroyed because from aerial photography it looked like a missile and the implication being that would draw strikes on to their forces in Zepa. Colonel Indic's -- he was never particularly helpful, and that was a sort of fairly typical flippant reply from Indic which I took to mean, why do we actually have to justify what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are due to have a break in four minutes' time in any case, so what I suggest is that we have the break. May I suggest, please, today, to limit our breaks to 20 minutes and then instead of 25, and then at the end we'll finish ten minutes earlier than usual. In other words, instead of finishing at quarter to 2.00, we'll finish at about half past 1.00 or a few minutes after that. All right? Agreed? Okay. So it's 20 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I certainly don't see Mr. Meek now. Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, he is working out of the office today and he will be with us tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I have an estimate, and the Defence team that seems to require most time is the Gvero Defence team. So Mr. Josse, I would suggest if you are in agreement that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've come to agreement with Madam Fauveau that she will go first. I will go second if that's agreeable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. Yes, Madam Fauveau? If you could kindly introduce yourself to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic and I am the Defence counsel of General Militic. You mentioned Colonel Indic earlier, can we say that he was your contact person within the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And Colonel Indic, was he able to organise meetings with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. He would generally be -- he'd be our first point of contact on that one in most cases and obviously it depended on Mladic's timetable, but, yes, Indic could do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember making a statement to the OTP in December of 2006?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm assuming the OTP is this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And where did you -- when you made this statement, you did it to the best of your recollection, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall that you described General Miletic as being the assistant chief of the General Miletic [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I've reread that statement and that's clearly what it says. I think at the time I referred to some handwritten notes which is probably where the date would have come from as well. Beyond that, I have to say I simply don't remember what that relationship was, and, yeah, I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my friend may be already on top of this but the transcript is unclear, and the translation I heard I think also leaves some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in fact, Mr. President, I wanted to correct line 16 and 17. I wanted to say in fact that General Miletic was described as being the deputy Chief of Staff of General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Are you following, Mr. Dibb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slightly confused but yes, I'm clear that that's what the -- how the statement reads from what I said virtually a year ago. However, what I'm saying is I simply now don't remember who -- whether he was Milosevic's Chief of Staff or Chief of Staff slightly further up the line. I don't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And to clarify, do you agree that General Milosevic was the Sarajevo Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. I think he was. Yes, I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right that today you have absolutely no recollection that you dealt with General Miletic or that there was a meeting that you had with him while you were in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No. I do remember -- I remember having the meeting, but I don't remember particularly the details of it or the dynamics of that meeting, who was -- who was taking a lead in it at all. It was -- it was a busy time and that was one of several meetings we had discussing the implementation of the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And those meetings took place in the month of September 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: To be honest, I couldn't tell you right now whether they did, but I know -- I did look at a written note which, if that's the date that came from that, then, yes. It would also make sense that bearing in mind when these events happened that that was when the meeting did take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2575, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you had a chance to look at these documents earlier, but is it right to say that before yesterday you had never seen these documents?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say because it's quite possible we got given this piece of paper as a -- to show to people at a check-point. That wouldn't be unusual. So I may well have seen the document. I certainly wouldn't have remembered detail on a -- whatever you want to call this for getting through a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that this document is not addressed to the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Looking at the message now, it a -- yes, it says, "To military posts," but again, if I recall how the system worked we would very often -- we would speak through the UNMO office in Pale to request documents such as this, to give passage through check-points. I think it was usual for us to receive a copy of such documents, but, yes, it's being addressed to the check-points to say let these guys move through.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there was another document addressed to the UNPROFOR, another document that the UNPROFOR had to have on them, the UNPROFOR members who were travelling had to have that document on them in order to show it to the control post?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's possible but I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But at any rate, you don't recall seeing this particular document prior to the day of yesterday, when it was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I don't. But I'll say again that doesn't mean that I didn't see it. It's just simply I don't recall seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you left for Zepa in July 1995, the delegation in which you were was carrying a sophisticated communications device, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. We had a TACSAT with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in order to get to Zepa, you had to go through Serb check-points; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you were able to go through these control points or these check-points carrying that sophisticated device?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: We clearly did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this sophisticated device was not declared to the Serb authorities, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Probably not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But at any rate, you had absolutely no problem to go through Serb check-points. You arrived at one point in Zepa, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. I would -- if we were being pernickety I can't remember if we had absolutely no problem but; however, we obviously did arrive in Zepa. Sorry, looking at the transcript, I'm not saying we did have problems, I'm just saying I can't say we had absolutely in problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell me what were the problems that you experienced to get to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. I don't -- I don't remember, but I'm not prepared to say we had absolutely no problem. It was pretty standard to have delays at check-points. And whether we call them problems or not, I don't recall if we did or didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that when you arrived at the observation post of the Ukrainian unit, you met with the Red Cross representatives?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. From my -- personally it was more of an informal yes, they were there, and we talked to them. So yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
