utterances.text: And when you arrived there, the Red Cross representatives, they were involved in the evacuation of the population of Zepa, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: When we arrived, the -- as I recall, the Red Cross representative was at the top of the hill with us talking to General Mladic and trying to get permission to move down into the village itself. Once there, as I mentioned earlier, she took a very stand-off view to it, saying she didn't want to be involved in what she termed ethnic cleansing, and if my memory serves me correctly, Red Cross had virtually no further part to play in Zepa itself but said they were going to concentrate their efforts in Kladanj and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But this was their decision, the Serbs never stopped them from entering villages around Zepa, right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: On this -- I can't vouch for what their relationship was with the Serbs on any other occasion, but on this case clearly they were let into the village and to the best of my knowledge, it was their decision not to participate further, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you asked General Mladic to allow you to go to the village of Zepa, you got that authorisation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you went down to the village in Zepa, were you escorted by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, I can't remember specifically. I am pretty certain that we were in the first vehicle down. I remember feeling somewhat anxious about the mine strike that was on the road. So my recollection is that we were in the lead vehicle. I know General Tolimir appeared down in the village some stage shortly afterwards. He may or may not have been part of that initial convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But in any case, when you were in the village, so once you were in the village, you were able to move around freely, the Serbs did not stop you from moving in Zepa. You had the freedom of movement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: For the first days, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you arrived in Zepa, did you hear that an agreement had been passed between the local population of Zepa and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No. I don't recall hearing that prior to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 6D30, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I showed you yesterday, when I met you, this agreement. Is it right that, in fact, prior to yesterday, you had never seen this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You do know, however, or you did know, that there were some negotiations that went on between the Serbs and the Muslims in Zepa, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: What I -- what do I remember is, on at least one and possibly two of the occasions when I went back up to check-point 2 at the top, General Smith plus Avdo Palic and the Serbs were discussing the issue of prisoner exchanges, prisoner swaps, and again what I recall, which is -- I wasn't party to the negotiation itself. I was aware they were taking place. My recollection is that one of the hang-ups that was taking place was that the Bosnian Muslim politicians in Sarajevo were saying something different from what Avdo Palic was saying. And I'm straying into supposition. I'm guessing there was issue on who was able to sign what.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall, when you gave your first statement to the OTP of this Tribunal, that was in 1997, and in that statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor on page 3, paragraph 4, you stated that the people were separated and that only women and children arrived in the village while the men remained in the mountain. Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to what you knew, the men who remained in the mountains, that was the decision of Muslim men, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that the Serbs would have preferred that these men go down to the village and that they give themselves up?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm simply not sure, simply not sure on that at all. If -- if we are talking about -- and again I'm straying into supposition, do you want me to follow it up or leave it where it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't object at first because I thought maybe there would be some personal basis upon which he could answer the question, but I think it's becoming clear that he feels like he may have to speculate. I think that the question is speculative at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Do you wish to comment on that, Madam Fauveau? Considering that he himself said and again I'm straying into a supposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I perfectly agree with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do not speculate. Please. I'm not asking to you do that. Could you please take a look at paragraph 2 of the agreement before you on the screen. Is it right to say that on paragraph 2, one can read the following. [In English] "Avdo Palic shall immediately issue an order to his troops to withdraw from the defence lines and to move together with the civilian population into the centres of populated area villages, they shall not attempt any illegal crossing to the territory of Republika Srpska"?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on paragraph 5 of this agreement, we can read as follows: "[In English] Avdo Palic shall immediately proceed with the disarmament of his units. All weapons from Zepa enclave shall be handed over to the representatives of the BSA in UNPROFOR base in Zepa."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what you knew regarding the Muslim unit that was around Zepa, that unit was not disarmed and they did not surrender; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, according to the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the Serbs allowed the evacuation of the civilian population, didn't they, even if that unit was not disarmed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've told us earlier that the buildings around Zepa or surrounding Zepa during the evacuation, I'm not talking about what happened after, so the buildings around Zepa, in the hills, were burning, and you yourself did not see who had started the fire to those buildings, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, sir, you've told us that you did not know if those were farms or houses, residences. Were you able to see these buildings?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we could see buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree to say that Zepa is surrounded by high hills and that you do not have lots of buildings in those high hills?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, not lots of buildings, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown document 6D29. You've mentioned earlier or you talked earlier about Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter. Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter, who is mentioned in paragraph 1 in this document, is he the deputy of -- or the assistant of General Smith?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Can I just quickly read through the document? And I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. I've read that and, yes, that Colonel Baxter mentioned here will be General Smith's MA.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The last sentence of the second paragraph states as follows: "[In English] Many houses in the hills were burning apparently torched by departing Bosnians."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter had absolutely no reason to draft an inexact or untrue report, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the top of the page, in order to see the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The date is the 26th of July 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: 26th July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated earlier that units of the Republika Srpska army had not entered the Zepa village when you went down to the village.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, they definitely -- they weren't in it at the time that we were there. I said it's probably impossible for me to say certainly whether they'd been in and been out, but certainly they weren't in it when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it right to say that during the entire evacuation process, you did not see a single Serb soldier in the Zepa village? I'm sorry, I believe that interpretation is not correct. What I wanted to ask the witness is that during the entire evacuation, you did not see a large amount of Serb soldiers in the Zepa village?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa, the Zepa village was not bombed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the civilian population in Zepa waiting to be evacuated was not subject to any firing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Certainly the population within the village, no. We did hear small arms fire in the surrounding hills but that wasn't directed at people in the village, as far as I could tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in the hills, there were the Muslim men who were part of the Zepa military unit, the Muslim military unit of Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the village of Zepa, you didn't see any active intimidation, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said earlier on that the population was very clearly frightened. Would you agree that in general, in the case of armed conflict, the civilian population is frightened?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I would certainly agree, yeah, that it's usual to be frightened. I would say that's not necessarily the whole -- the whole story or the whole answer here. I'm not sure if you're going to pursue that or whether I should pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Perhaps you could continue. I'm sure that you agree that the war in Bosnia was a particularly brutal civil war?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah definitely. It was a brutal civil war, and I think we have to view what happened in Zepa within that wider context. Taking into account it happened pretty much towards the end of it. My recollection is that people were aware of what had happened in Srebrenica shortly before, and that was influencing their thinking.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But if we don't talk about the events in Srebrenica, the events in Srebrenica were brutal, and the war was brutal as well?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. I accept as, you know, across the whole conflict on, you know, throughout and on all sides, there was an immense brutality and that was well known to the civilian population across the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the fear that the civilian population in Zepa felt as regards the events occurring towards the end of the war, following a series of other brutal events on all sides, was something that -- well, unfortunately we can say that it was a natural fear in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It was, but as I mentioned earlier, what was -- what sets it slightly apart but again probably not unusual within the Bosnian context, is that it was fear of what happened once the fighting stopped rather than fear of the fighting itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the purpose of a war is to take territory? This is in general terms, the usual purpose of a war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection to this question per se. I'm -- I would ask what the relevance is going to be to this witness's testimony, especially if we are going to continue along a theoretical line. I mean generally I don't have a problem with engaging in some of these discussions, but I'd like to know where we are going, especially given the time considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll move on to another question, but I'm somewhat stupified that the OTP in this line of questioning does not understand the relevance, but I'll leave it at that. I'll say no more in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next question, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that during the evacuation in Zepa, you saw no act perpetrated by the Serbian armed forces that could lead to an increase in fear among the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't think so, while the -- while the body of civilians were still within the village, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The Serbian forces, in fact, did everything to avoid causing fear among the population. For instance, they didn't enter the village?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. It was in that early phase, while the people were there, it was well-organised and well-disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to what you know, they allowed the Red Cross to enter, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: They did, indeed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: They also allowed for the arrival of additional units from the UNPROFOR, the French units arrived, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: They did. I don't remember exactly when, but I'm sure they arrived subsequent to my own arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And while you were in the Zepa village, you were able to contact the Muslim civilian population, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. We were able to walk freely amongst them and indeed had to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And it was possible for you to reassure them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It was, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the civilian affairs, civil affairs representatives even tried to draw up a list of the people waiting to be evacuated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. That was all fairly ad hoc. As I'd said before, I'd initially hoped that, perhaps naively, that it would have been done by the Red Cross. What I do remember very clearly was that I probably spent slightly more time with the people around the buses than the civil affairs lot, and on one of the big -- the big movements, I was actually getting a representative of the population to assist with filling out lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, there was no Serbian intervention, interference in your work as were you carrying it out in the village of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that you've already said that the civilian population in Zepa very clearly wanted to leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And as far as you're concerned, nobody came to see you to say that they wanted to stay?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The -- in the only one was that old man I mentioned at the end, who again just wasn't entirely clear what was going on around him, and I do remember him sort of running back and saying, well, crikey, I forgot to lock my door and thinking, you know, reality is that's not something you've got to worry about, but I'm fairly sure he didn't particularly want to move, but did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, did you not see anybody being forced to board one of the buses?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the international forces themselves asked the Serbs to send more vehicles in order to be able to evacuate everybody?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. That was -- I mean that was just part of a coordination function, and that the Serb forces had laid on vehicles and there were people who wanted to get on to those vehicles so, on possibly the third morning, it was one where General Tolimir had said, look, I'll give you guys a shout in the morning with regard to sending vehicles. Nothing happened. You know, the people -- we had no means of providing food to the people in the village at that stage. It was pretty hot. It was pretty miserable so, yeah, we knew that the vehicles were waiting at the top of the hill, and we said we are ready to receive them now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On that day of July of 1995 aside from that evacuation, was there anything else that could have been done for the population in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again I'm going to be -- we can speculate. There is lots that -- there is lots that could have been done. As, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in the area of speculation. Please, let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that in July 1995, evacuation of the civilian population in Zepa was the best solution for that population?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think you'd have to ask the -- you'd have to ask the population that. It was an option. It wasn't necessarily the only option. I'm not prepared to say it was the best one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the evacuation was well-organised?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It was organised in a civilised fashion, to the extent that this was possible in the middle of the war in Bosnia in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, yeah, it was a difficult time and they, as I recall it, there were more buses than trucks so yes, they did try to make it as civilised as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that once everybody had been evacuated from the village, the Ukrainians went to see whether there were any civilians in the mountains?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. I think that probably happened at some stage prior to the departure of the final 400 but, yes, we made efforts before the whole thing closed to make sure that to the best of our knowledge, all the civilians had been found and evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the Serbs did not prevent the Ukrainians from trying to find the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. We didn't participate in those particular patrols, but all the reports we received was that they were able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As far as you know, once the evacuation had been carried out, the Serbs did not embark upon major -- in major conflict with the Muslim men remaining in the mountains?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, no. But I simply don't know, as you know we left some days afterwards. Prior to that we'd heard some small arms fire but nothing that sounded like a major confrontation or conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Smith was present in the Zepa sector, he was at the Ukrainian units's observation point during at least part of the evacuation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. On, I think, three occasions, he came as far as OP 2. He never actually went into the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But he knew how this evacuation was being organised?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And he didn't have any comments to make as regards the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said earlier on that there was a Ukrainian captain who said to you that the Zepa mosque had been destroyed after your departure?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that you left together with the Ukrainian forces when you left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: My recollection is that we left with some but not all, and I do think that's reflected in the statement as well, that some of them stayed behind. There was a slightly peculiar standoff towards the end, where I think it was Kusic saying, Listen, I've got unfinished business with the Ukrainians so most of you push off and get out of here, but I want to finish off with these guys. So I think when we left, we left with part but not all of the Ukrainian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Dibb, my name is David Josse and I'm asking questions on behalf of Milan Gvero. I want to begin by asking you some questions about your job with General Smith. Did you, when you were at the residence, see him on a daily basis, assuming he was there of course?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you attend most of the meetings he went to?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: A lot. I mean, the day, the day began with a sort of morning prayers which was a briefing to quite a wide collection of people, which in various, each contingent would have somebody, so I attended that. There was then a smaller meeting afterwards which I attended regularly. I attended most, I would say, of the meetings with the Bosnian Serbs, Emma Bliss would have covered more of the meetings with the Bosnian Muslim government in Sarajevo itself, and meetings with civil affairs people, I would not necessarily have attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Emma Bliss speak or read Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, and no doubt better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And she was a British officer?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I would like you to fit Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter into the picture. He was, you've told us, General Smith's military assistant. What did that involve, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: He would -- I mean, to some extent he's a sounding board for the general. Somebody he can bounce ideas off. He covered slightly demeaning to the role to say he helped set up meetings. He was -- sorry, he was above that but would have -- would have recommendations and passed stuff down to Captain Bliss and myself. He would often attend meetings with the general, high level meetings, and assist or actually personally do the note taking thereafter for those meetings. Drafting of letters on behalf of the general. And the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What sort of communication or memoranda were you privy to or perhaps I might be easier for you to answer that the other way around. What were you not privy to by reason of your rank as against General Smith's?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I didn't have secret clearance, but I think Captain Bliss may have. Certainly stuff I didn't have access to later on was target lists, for instance, sites that were going to be hit, I didn't have. But otherwise, it was fairly free discussions. So I could -- fairly sure I would have been shown copies of memoranda taken at meetings, certainly with the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to be precise about your job, you were a liaison officer with the Bosnian Serbs; is that right? Or with both sides to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's specifically to the Bosnian Serbs, but as I hinted at earlier things got quite difficult communication wise after air strikes in May 2000 -- 1995. Part of what I was doing was, again, backwards and forwards in and out of Sarajevo escorting people into town which involved crossing through Bosnian Muslim check-points, so -- which is fairly low level communication that I would be speaking with them to make sure that wheels were oiled so we could get in and out, but I do remember attending one meeting with the general and Izetbegovic. I can't particularly remember what was discussed, and I can't remember why Captain Bliss didn't attend. She may well have been on leave but that was an exception rather than the norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've described communications becoming difficult in May of 2005 [sic]. Smith and Mladic stopped speaking to one another, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't think it's quite as simple as that. It -- from my point of view what changed is I could get through as far as Lukavica barracks, but thereafter it was -- there was no way we are letting you go through to Pale and talk. I'm pretty sure Smith -- well, I know that Smith wanted to speak more with Mladic, and didn't speak as much as he would have wished. My feeling at the time was also the military were very unwilling for us to go and speak to the political side in Pale which is why we kept hitting that wall at Lukavica and were unable to get access. So literally the next time I was physically in Pale was the day of the mortar landing in the marketplace in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you say that Smith had a deliberate policy or plan as to how he was going to deal with Mladic in May and June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'd far rather you ask General Smith that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I will do but I'd like to know your opinion bearing in mind how closely you worked with them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sure. He was an extremely bright man as would you hope dealing with an officer of that rank and position, he was an extremely impressive man to work with and for, and I'm perfectly sure that he -- yes, he would have had a plan. I'm far from sure I'm entirely aware of what his plan was at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's really what I'm coming to. Why wouldn't you have been aware? And I ask you that as someone who has got no military experience. Explain why it is that he wouldn't have conveyed that to you? It may seem a stupid question. And I'm being told to slow down a bit so I'm going to deliberately do that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I would say he -- firstly I'm not sure who he actually discussed the plan with in all its details, and he may well have done a lot of that thinking on his own. I would say there was a risk in telling me, in that I spent a fair bit of time backwards and forwards to the -- on to the Serb side. They had in -- sorry, whenever it was, when the bombing took place in May, they -- the BSA had kidnapped, for want of a better word, some of the military observers, chained them to ammunition bunkers. So people were being put under stress, and it's quite possible that why put me in a position where I had anything like that which I may have revealed which he didn't wish to be revealed? But I have to say that is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on slightly. We know that General Smith was on leave from the 1st of July to the 8th of July. He then went to a meeting in Geneva, I think on that date, with the Secretary-General, and he then went back on leave either that day or the following day, I'm not exactly certain, and his leave was eventually aborted on the 11th of July. First of all, do you have any recollection of him going on leave at that time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. I do. In the -- in the very broadest -- in the broadest terms, and I'm aware that the -- towards the end the rapid reaction force started to move up while General Smith was on leave. Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the rapid reaction force in a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are moving too fast. If you could first allow a short pause between question and answer because the interpreters have to translate both into French and into Serbo-Croat so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please try to cooperate, as much as you can. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Dibb, was there any discussion, and by discussion I mean murmurs of surprise, among the junior officers as to the fact that Smith was away at such a critical time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not that I recall but that's not to say that there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As best as you can recall, did it cross your mind that this was a surprising time for him to be away, and in particular it was surprising that he wasn't recalled from leave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes and no. In that as I've said before, he was -- he was no doubt and still is, you know, a brilliant man. He thinks things through, and I had complete confidence in him as a commander. Yes, it did seem to me that your man's on leave and all the stuff is happening, slightly odd. But I was happy that he, whenever he went on leave he took a communications team with him, so he was obviously going to be briefed on what was happening. And he knows the business of soldiering or knew the business of soldiering a lot better than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you say communications team, he too had some sophisticated communications equipment --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- with him?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'd like to ask you briefly about your perception of General Smith's relationship with some of the other senior officers that he worked with. Did you have much to do with General Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Personally, no. I met him on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What language did you communicate with him in?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Oh, I certainly don't speak French, so I'm not sure if we worked through an interpreter or not. I simply don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever meet General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same question about communication and language?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think Janvier was probably addressed in English, but again I'm not -- I'm simply not certain on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've already told us that Janvier was Smith's direct commander?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent did you see Janvier give orders to Smith?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not a lot that I saw but, again, coming back to your earlier question on what was I privy to and what was I not, a Smith-Janvier conversation was definitely not something that I would have been privy to. I'm very confident that they talked and that they had a good relationship. I believe they had come across each other previously in perhaps gulf war 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any tension between those two men as to whether air strikes should take place and if so to what extent?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I remember feeling a lot of tension myself on that issue but now, I simply -- I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just going to ask for some clarification because air strikes, close air support, had been requested and actually executed on a number of occasions. I didn't know whether that would make a difference to the answer, but he's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what about General Gobillard? He took charge in that period in early July when General Smith was away, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: He no doubt was given, yeah, given control of matters in Sarajevo at that stage. I don't recall the exact ins and outs of what level of authorisation General Gobillard held vis-a-vis Smith. He was at the end of TACSAT somewhere not too far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you able to help us as to why Gobillard took charge at that point rather than Smith's Chief of Staff Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not particularly but I have a suspicion Gobillard was the senior officer of the two. He was a two star, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that is right, I can help to you that extent. I think the answer --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at that point in time, did you work closely with General Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, not particularly. In fact, I don't recall getting any direct taskings from General Gobillard at a personal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to some of the matters that you have dealt with in your evidence. When you were in Zepa, did you have any personal conversation with General Smith?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but I would say certainly I will have talked to him, without question I will have talked to him when I went up the hill and saw him and the team at the top of the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you able to communicate with him by means of the sophisticated equipment that you had with you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, we could have. I don't think we spoke to him directly and it would probably have been quite unusual to have him at the end of the -- personally at the end of it, but if we had said we need to speak to the boss himself, I'm quite sure that would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just a little bit on there equipment, you used a word for it earlier which I wasn't familiar with and the stenographer didn't pick up. Could you give that word again slowly please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think it was called a TACSAT, T-A-C-S-A-T.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. If any of the questions I'm about to pose to you, you feel you don't want to answer by reason of security, then certainly for my part, say, and I will almost most certainly move on. We've seen in the document signed by General Miletic that you went to Srebrenica -- I beg your pardon, to Zepa, with two members of the British Special Forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Josse. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Srebrenica, just to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. I was right the first time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the presence of any member of the British Special Forces in Srebrenica prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah. There was definitely one of my -- somebody I knew on the language course at Ekensfield [phoen] was attached to a JCO team in Srebrenica and their OP came under direct tank fire during the Srebrenica clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This was obviously prior to your getting there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, it will have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And other than these -- let he me start again. Do you know how many members of the Special Forces were there at that point?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we know, don't we, that the forces who were there were Dutch?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the most general sense, are you able to help us with what those British forces were doing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Observing and reporting back, I would say, in the most general sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. That will do for my purposes. Do you know, did they have sophisticated radio equipment with them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I would have been surprised if they didn't but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And who would they report back to? Again, general answer. I don't want any operational details.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: They would have reported down the JCO net.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to state the obvious, General Smith was aware they were there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I would have thought so but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In fact, yes, he certainly did know they were there, on that, second thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I am going to ask the next question which is this: Bearing this in mind, why was it that the residence didn't know exactly what was going on in Srebrenica? In the early part of July, the first two weeks of July, shall we say?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm simply not sure what General Smith did or didn't know, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you presumably, you didn't go to Geneva with him on the 8th of July for the meeting with the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you presumably were simply told that he'd gone back on leave and you in no way contributed to that decision?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like briefly to turn to Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter, please. Where was he the first two weeks of July, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, I don't recall. I'm assuming he was in -- still in the residency but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you went to Zepa, we know he didn't come with you. That's Mr. Baxter I'm talking about, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did he go to Zepa with General Smith, any idea?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think he did. I think he probably went up to the top of the hill. Is that related in my statement or not? Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know off-hand. I'll let others check if they would be so kind, and I'll move on. I think you've said, and I'm now moving specifically to Zepa, that you had no specific recollection as to when the French reinforcements arrived?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But it was after you arrived and you arrived on which date, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, what I have to say on dates is that I'm now going purely by what's written in my earlier statement, which indicates we arrived on the 25th. I think that they came after us. But I wouldn't swear blind to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A few matters, if I may, going back in time. As the liaison officer, you presumably were privy to Serb complaints about the non-demilitarisation of the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that discussions on that were on going and yes, I was aware there were complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What did you do about those complaints?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: If the process was that if these complaints were or if -- if I was attending a meeting that was not attended by General Smith or Colonel Baxter, on completion of that meeting, I would go back and have a full and open debrief on what had been discussed. So if a complaint was made to me verbally rather than on a piece of paper, at a meeting, I would have gone back and said, this is the message that's come from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at one, if we may. This is 6D163. I understand, Madam Registrar, that there are two documents with that number in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just ask my friend if they could distribute the list of cross-examination documents which we've not received? We received one hard copy document, but we've not received a list yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From none of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From a couple of Defence teams. I frankly don't know which Defence teams have cross. We've received three lists -- two lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's an error on our part. It's been sent to all the Defence lawyers but not the Prosecution. I'm sorry, it's a pure error and I've got a hard copy here that my learned friend can have, so he's got one to follow. That is an oversight, and I repeat, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is any other Defence team that hasn't done that as yet, please, I know that Madam Fauveau last time had indicated that she had already. So -- okay. Let's proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the one dated the 21st of May. It's not this document. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this is the first page, Mr. Dibb, and we can see it's a confidential report from Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter of a meeting between General Smith and Dr. Karadzic, 21st of May. And number 1 says they met in hotel near Pale. Could we turn to the second page and to item number 4, please? "The eastern enclaves. On the issue of the enclaves, Karadzic maintained the UN had failed to implement any of the previous agreements relating to the eastern enclaves" -- mentions Western Slavonia, but I'll read on. "Karadzic accepted the UN had been a moderating influence especially in the light of the military potential of the enclaves. Again, he asserted he could not respect the safe area mandates as the enclaves were effectively safe havens or the ARBiH. He said he expected the BiH to attempt to break out of one of the enclaves and he expected UNPROFOR to be caught in the cross-fire. The enclaves, he said, are a time bomb about to explode. He maintained the UN should get out, but also that UNHCR would be safe to remain. UNPROFOR presence he stated was welcome, 'Only if the enclaves were demilitarised and become safe areas for civilian population.'" That type of complaint was quite common from the Bosnian Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. I would say it was probably an ongoing theme for some of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my question to you, as the person tasked with liaising with these very people, is what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. You personally, sir.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I wasn't in a position to make a decision that would influence it so I was simply able to, as I said before, if I received reports that the general hadn't received personally, I would pass them on to the general. Otherwise, it certainly wasn't up to me to make any decision that would demilitarise these enclaves. Likewise, if Smith had a comment back that he -- which I don't recall him having which he didn't wish to convey in person, I would have gone back and dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent was it your job or position to advise either Smith, Baxter, or indeed Nicolai that this was a complaint of the people you were liaising with and that something needed to be done about it, or do I miss characterise your role?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think slightly you do miss characterise it. It -- yes we would advise and again, as I've said before, General Smith was a man who -- he knew where he was going. He was an extraordinary man to deal with in that there were meetings where I -- I would come with a suggestion, and I remember on one occasion, we ended up -- a decision taken was 180 degrees different from the recommendation I'd made, but he still was able to make me feel that the contribution had been relevant. So there was nothing in the command style which discouraged us passing on recommendations, but on something at a level as high as this, when everyone was patently aware of the issues, it certainly wasn't for me to say I think you've got your strategy wrong, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've said that General Smith was a man who knew where he was going. Did you know at that time where he was going and if so, where, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I don't think I knew -- I don't think I did know exactly where he was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Prior to your arrival in Zepa, were you aware of the terrain in that area?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In the broadest terms, yes. I mean, it's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when you got there, you saw the terrain. Could you describe it to the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: As with much of central Bosnia, it's very hilly and very wooded. As I mentioned before, a single track leading down to the village itself. A river just outside the village. In saying thickly wooded there are, if I recall correctly, there were areas of more open pasture land as well, areas where cattle would be able to graze.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you have accepted, in the evidence you've given hitherto, that the passage of time clearly affects your memory. It's almost -- it's over 12 years since the events that you're describing took place.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And obviously, you quite properly and fairly looked at your witness statement over the last day or two in order to jog your memory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you would accept, I suppose, that passage of time can also play tricks on memory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And let me follow that up by asking you a little bit about the rapid reaction force that you mentioned earlier. Who was the commander of that force?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'd say in reality it would probably turn out to be General Smith, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But he didn't want people to know that he was the commander of it, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think that probably is fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why was that, as far as you could make out at the time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Saying is it fair? As, you know, as you've alluded to there was the whole issue of, you know, General Smith being on leave, rapid reaction force, rapid reaction force moving up. I know deputy Chief of Staff Colonel Coiffet was involved in bringing it all forward. As far as -- I'd say as far as I was personally aware, my view was, as I've said earlier, Smith would have been at the end of a communications device, being briefed on exactly what was happening. So he would -- he would certainly have known and again I'm speculating as to what I remembered back then, but I would have been surprised if the force had been employed rather than deployed, without his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going back a couple of months to the arrival of the force, I think it was, correct me if I'm wrong, April May of 1995. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware that General Smith was anxious that the rapid reaction force vehicles were not painted white and didn't have UN markings?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's simply not a -- it's not a detail that I remember now as to whether or not that was the policy or whether it was his, General Smith's wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you given any instructions as to what if anything to say to the Bosnian Serbs about the rapid reaction force at the time of its arrival in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of being asked about it by Colonel Indic or any other Bosnian Serb you liaised with?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't remember specifics. I'd be surprised if they weren't asking about it. But I simply don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in that regard, had General Smith given you any instructions as to what to say to them about the force and/or his, General Smith's involvement in it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not that I'm -- again, not that I recall. And if I can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes of course.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: -- something, as he was the senior military commander in Bosnia, so it shouldn't really have been a surprise to anyone that General Smith was actually the commander of that force. Whether he was the -- he wasn't the unit commander obviously because he was at a higher level in the command structure, but all forces deployed in Bosnia would have come under his control. Otherwise you've got a split command within the theatre, which wouldn't have made a great deal of sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try and avoid building an argument in your own mind to try and see into it. It's a question of whether you knew or you didn't know, and in this case, you say that you don't seem to recall. So let's move ahead, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have told us a bit about the Ukrainian Battalion, and you clearly formed a very low impression of that battalion, particularly when they tried to steal your vehicle, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Steal from the vehicle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From the vehicle, I beg your pardon. But my question is: You clearly formed a very low opinion of them at that point.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Before that point, before the stealing of the vehicle issue, it was -- conditions in the camp were way below the standard I would have expected of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: -- people who have had time on their hands to keep things tidy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my question is, were you aware of these problems prior to your arrival in the enclave; in other words, was it something that was said officially or otherwise around the residency about the deficiencies of there particular battalion?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I don't think and I'm not sure if anyone had actually been into Zepa itself to come back and say, crikey, these guys are not quite up to the standard. I think it's fair to say that there was a degree of, call it arrogance, call it whatever you want, that NATO forces would believe that NATO forces are better than others, just as regimental pride takes a part in saying we are better than the other ones, whether based on fact or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And, for example, when they tried to pilfer from your vehicle, did you challenge any of their officers?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't think we did on that particular occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Because it didn't come as a surprise to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What, that your fellow soldiers were trying to steal from you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: People on your side?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, looking at the general condition of the camp, it didn't strike us as -- I mean, yes, it's disappointing but the whole thing was in, as I said, pretty ropey condition. And so it wasn't a surprise that soldiers were -- had such poor discipline, and if you bear in mind the gravity of the situation that we found ourselves in, somebody who got chewed out the back of a Land Rover without taking anything didn't amount to much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were the Ukrainian Battalion able to provide you with any information about the military operation of the Bosnian Muslim troops within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, I think they must have been, but I don't remember detail of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D81, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dibb, this is the first of a number of documents in B/C/S, as we call it here, that I'm going to show you. This -- most of them I'm glad to say have translations. It's up to you whether you want to look at them in the original or the English translation. This particular document is a document dated the 2nd of July, from a man called Mr. Gusic, chief of communications in the Zepa Brigade, to a -- to the 28th Division chief of communication. Paragraph number 5 says "There is no major problems in work, a minor problem is the fact that we had to move the CV, communications centre, to the hospital basement because of enemy shelling and the quality of transmission is now quite poor." Were you aware of anything like that happening? In other words, that via Bosniak forces had moved their communications centre into a hospital?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I certainly wasn't aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next break, Mr. Josse, is due at 12.30, but if you wish to stop earlier, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next invite you to have a look at 6D82. This is again in the same language but, in fact, is a Serb document from a Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric to the -- among other things, the Main Staff, and also to the forward command post of the Drina Corps. And at the bottom of the first page in the English, there is a description which says, "For four days now, the Muslims have been making their presence known." And it lists various weaponry which I'm not going to read out. Perhaps you'd read it to yourself and tell me if you were aware of that sort of weaponry being used and being at the disposal of the Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: What I'd say is I don't -- I don't personally, or I don't think I knew or had been briefed on what exactly the Zepa Brigade had with them. That type of weaponry fairly common across Bosnia at the time and in possession of the army of BiH. So I'm afraid that slightly avoids the answer. I can't recall. I don't think I knew specifically they had it. I'm not surprised now to read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And perhaps my final question before the break is: Were you aware, when you arrived in Zepa, the extent to which there had been heavy fighting between the VRS and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I think we'd been aware of a -- of a buildup, and it's something that -- it's fair to say we'd been expecting, that in the enclaves we're vulnerable throughout and everybody knew that, events happened in Srebrenica, the enclaves were -- yes, I'm sure we were aware that there had been conflict building up to something and no surprise particularly to learn that Zepa had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But specifically, in the days before you arrived, I want to suggest there had been heavy fighting. Did you have any knowledge of that? Did the Ukrainians tell you, for example?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, I simply don't -- I don't recall now. My guess is yes but I simply don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take the break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse, and thank you, Mr. Dibb. We'll have a 20-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse. And we'll be finishing at around about 1.30, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've alluded, Mr. Dibb, to the fact that you were aware, when you were in Zepa, that there was some ongoing fighting even after the departure of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: What I recall is that there was small arms fire, which right now I have to say I don't remember if that was the first days while the civilians were there or the period afterwards. Yes, small arms fire, which doesn't necessarily mean it was aimed at anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what you're saying is you can't remember exactly when it was and you recall no more than small arms fire?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a summary of what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 6D136, please? Could we scroll down this, please? Next page. Number 4 -- number D at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So this is a sit-rep report of the 30th of July. We see that it says, "Update from Zepa. Four UNMOs remain in the Zepa pocket and have remained -- beg your pardon, and have maintained regular contact with UNMO HQ at Sarajevo." Do you know who those four UNMOs were, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going on, "A separate report will be released through the MIO net covering the detailed information provided by the team in Zepa. The team are currently located at OP 2 and have been restricted to this location since arrival in the pocket. Team stated that a French delegation entered Zepa town today and have confirmed that UNMO" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "Equipment is still with UKRCOY, attempts will be made to extract this equipment. 31st July. Team reported hearing intensive shelling on 29th of July, 23 explosions, 8 HM G bursts and four to six outgoing mortar rounds but could not confirm firing points and impact areas. Team did not hear any firing activity today." So this relates to the 29th of July specifically.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's more than small arms fire, is it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It is, if it's talking about artillery and mortars, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you had no knowledge of that going on whilst you were in the pocket, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Certainly not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because what I want to suggest, but I think it's fair to say you're unable to comment on this, is that there was heavy fighting still going on in parts of the enclave on the 29th of July, well after the civilians had departed.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's, as you say, it's possible, but I am unable to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dibb, you've given evidence about your recollection that you had become aware by this time of the events in Srebrenica, and you have gone on to say that you thought that the civilian population of Zepa was so aware. At the time, who had you discussed that with?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, no recollection. If I was aware, it would have been because it was coming through in a much higher channel than myself and had passed down to me rather than from me to pass up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You say if I was aware. Why do you use the word "if," please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, I don't remember specifically the day that I did become aware of these incidents. In my recollection is that I was aware of it prior to deploying to Zepa. I'm pretty certain that I was aware of it prior to deploying to Zepa, and that -- it was part of my understanding of the whole rationale for being sent there was because something had gone wrong in Srebrenica, and it was to prevent that happening in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you have any briefing on the subject with General Smith or Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you returned to Sarajevo, I think you gave a briefing on what you had seen on the 3rd of August at the BH command?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you mention the state of knowledge as to what had happened to the men of Srebrenica in the course of that briefing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are there any notes of that briefing available?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Probably not. I would guess it was going in and giving a verbal brief after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going back to the time you were in the enclave, did you discuss this issue with Ed Joseph?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were working closely alongside him, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes and no. I would say that Ed and Viktor were to some extent running things, and I was doing much more down in the weeds making sure things went right, getting people on to vehicles. Yes we would have had discussions on any relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's inconceivable, isn't it, that you would have known about the fate of the men in Srebrenica and that he, Ed Joseph, would not have known. Would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to suggest that you're perhaps mistaken about this and that passage of time, memory has played tricks, and there was no clear information at that time as to what had happened to these unfortunate men in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: If you've got documents to show it, perhaps that is the case. If there was no clear information, that suggests there was still suspicion that something had happened, and it may well be that there was a suspicion that something had happened, but I am very clear that the decision to send a different team to Zepa was because there was either knowledge or suspicion that something had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time as to the extent to which the men of Srebrenica featured in the discussions either at a local level, that is between Torlak -- who I think whose name has not been mentioned, but he was a local civilian leader and Mladic, or at the national level, between Izetbegovic, Muratovic, and the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's again back to the exact timing of it, it's certainly, as we all know, became an issue that was talked about. Right now, I can't say whether it was an Izetbegovic-Muratovic issue to Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It certainly became an issue and that's why we're all here.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But the question is what you knew at the time, and well, you've heard my suggestion and I'll move on. The next issue I'd like to ask you about, please, relates to the -- both the looting and some of the destruction that you saw. You've described successful efforts by VRS officers to prevent their troops entering the enclave until the civilians had been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you've described thereafter seeing troops enter and loot and set fire to some buildings?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are a few documents I'd like to show you in this regard. And I mention this both to you and to the learned judges. Your Honour, the position is this, these documents that I'm about to show have not been translated. I'm not clear whether the witness is in a position to read the small extracts that I would like to ask him about, aloud, so that they can be translated but if the witness is unable -- I was going to come up with another suggestion but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But if the witness is unable to do that what we were going to suggest on behalf of General Gvero is that my legal assistant was going to read out those relevant passages and they could then be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Perhaps we have a third suggestion. I was just handed a copy of this, this wasn't on the list a little while ago, I don't know if it's possible give a copy to the Court interpreters so that they can read it directly rather than have yet another level involved here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. They've been give and copy in fact but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, I don't suppose the entire documents are going to be read. I would imagine that parts --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. I would have thought bits are going to have to be read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think your first suggestion to have your legal assistant read out the relevant parts would be perfect for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the document be placed on the ELMO to begin with, please? And I'm also going to give the witness a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you said they have not yet been translated but are they in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This one is not in e-court. The other one I'm going to refer to is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One moment, Mr. Josse, because we still need to have the ELMO adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Dibb, perhaps --?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I go on because I'm just going to deal with the background of the document. The witness has a hard copy there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is an order, isn't it, Mr. Dibb, we see the word "order" about eight lines down on the first page, that purports to come from General Mladic, it's dated the 30th of July of 1995, and it looks in the right-hand corner, handwritten, that he's sending it to the command of the Drina Corps. Do you agree with what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: If you just give me a minute to look through it. Okay. I'd definitely like to see or have translated more of it, but in general terms, yes, fire away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are going to do that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you also agree that immediately before the word "order," which is the word spelled N-A-R-E-D-J-U-J-E-M, is the preamble that really says that this sets out the responsibility of certain units of the VRS during the -- a declared state of war and it cites various ordinances?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Can we get that preamble read out to me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's start with that, please. Could that be done, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Pursuant to Article 175 of the law on the army and the decision of the president of the republic on the proclamation of the state of war, number 01-1473/95 dated 28th July 1995, with a view to ensuring conditions for the full and complete execution of combat tasks of the army units, I hereby order the following."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then moving on from the preamble it's item 6 which is the bottom of that first page, and then item 7 in due course on the top of the following page that I'd like to draw your attention to, and I'm going to ask to be read out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We forbid that any materiel be taken from the war zone irrespective of its ownership and origin without special approval of the logistics organ of the corps commands. "Especially from the areas from which the civilian population had moved out and been evacuated. The material goods that are attempted to be taken out from the zone of war without a special approval of the logistics organs of the corps commands shall be seized immediately and handed over for safekeeping at locations identified by corps commands in cooperation with the War Presidency of the municipalities. "As for the seized property, their certificates will be issued on these goods. The goods and people in transit should be inspected. In case of suspicious goods, persons from which these goods have been seized, should be issued a certificate on the temporarily seized goods. "Article 7, in the war zones, the collected cattle should not be slaughtered and misappropriated in any way. The command of the army units, in cooperation with the War Presidencies of the municipalities, will collect the abandoned cattle and other material goods. In the municipalities from which the civilian population has been moved out or evacuated, the cattle will be fed in an organised manner and all the material goods will be protected. "Article 18, the last page of the document" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Article 18 or 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's 18, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have to move a few further pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "If anybody fails to carry out orders as per this decision, they will be prosecuted before a competent military court."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Dibb, would you agree that what you've just heard purports to be an order not do exactly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes. It does -- it implies that -- it would be quite nice to see it in English written but that cattle and things are to be collected and looked after. I guess my question on it would be what happened to everything once it left?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, what you've described doesn't accord with this document; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: What I saw was stuff being put into vehicles and driven out of town, furniture, electrical appliances, and live stock and, yeah, there is absolutely no question at all that that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I conclude, I'd like to invite you also to have a look at some extracts from the diary or log of another witness in this case. His name was Colonel Trivic. Did you come across him?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Romanija Brigade, and he also was present at various times in Zepa and was engaged in action there. This is a harder document still because it's handwritten document in Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's 2D125, Your Honour. What has happened is, I understand, that parts of it are in evidence and those parts have been translated. Unfortunately, the bits that I wish to refer to have not been translated, whether they are technically in evidence or not perhaps doesn't matter. And the first page, please, is page 62 of that document. And this is an extract, I know it's not quite up yet, dated the 26th of July. Excuse me a moment. I'm going to ask Mr. Sladojevic to read a short part of this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
