utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I absolutely forbid the setting fire to houses." This paragraph has an exclamation mark beside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, I don't want to embarrass you, but is your language good enough?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: From the translation, my reading of Cyrillic handwritten is pretty shabby, [Interpretation] "Most strictly forbidden." [In English] I'm happy with that, yeah. It might say that but it didn't stop houses being burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At what point was that that the houses were burned?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Within the town itself, I would probably say from the day that people -- that the last people left. I remember walking down to the bridge and feeling the heat coming off the houses that had been burnt as I walked down the road. I also remember sitting there and asking the troops why this had happened or why they had done it, to which, you know, one -- you could hear the fire crackling away and the wood popping, as it does, and one of them saying, well, listen -- listen to that pop, you can hear there are mines in the house which was complete nonsense. And somebody else was -- well, the pop, the popping certainly wasn't a mine going off. And somebody else saying, well we burnt it because the fighting is over. And you know, it -- it happened and there is no -- absolutely no doubt in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next extract, please, which is on page 65, same date, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "9.45 hours, the order of the command of the Drina Corps that he strictly forbids the burning of houses, responsible are the brigade Commanders."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So again on the face of it, that order was disobeyed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the final extract, please, is on the following page and I think the following day, page 66, 27th of July. This is towards the bottom of the page, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "At 1030 hours, the setting fire of houses and marking the line of the brigade."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't actually understand that. Was he saying that was happening or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are stuck with what it says there and what the translation is, but what I'd like to ask you is whether the setting fire of certain items featured as part of a military tactic by either side to the battle?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Can I ask for a clarification of what you mean by certain items?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, anything.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: A house?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A house.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's -- it was quite -- as we all know, it was fairly common practice that villages would be left burnt to the ground or certain houses were left burnt to the ground. In this instance, and again I stray, I'd say my military assessment was there was absolutely no tactical reason to burn the houses. The question then comes, was there a strategic reason or was it down to sheer indiscipline? But there was no tactical benefit that I could see in burning those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What's the difference between tactical and strategic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Tactical would be to win that particular battle, shall we say. The taking of Zepa, Zepa was taken, it wasn't as if burning that house would have given them a field of fire, for instance, forward to suppress an enemy there or whatever. Whereas strategic would be, you know, for instance, let's leave the place impossible for people to return to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Now, I, you know, I can't see a tactical reason. I simply don't know if there was a strategic reason. The documents we've seen before clearly indicate there are orders that these things shouldn't happen. But they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you get any sense that there might be some sort of scorched earth policy going on in relation to the retreating Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Across the country or in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well in Zepa, but if your experiences across the country help you, then tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Probably varied from place to place, and in some and I would say to an extent on all sides, villages were razed. What I'm not able to say is was that a command that came down from, say, a General Mladic level or was it down to a local commander's level? It certainly -- it wasn't unusual to find villages that were completely smashed and that some of that damage had occurred afterwards. What I also seem to have in the back of my mind is that there was talk about rehousing displaced Bosnian Serbs back into villages, and following through the logic on that, it wouldn't make a great deal of sense to burn the whole of Zepa if there was a plan to put other displaced people into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And would that perhaps be a reason for the retreating Bosniaks to torch their own property knowing that they were going to have to abandon it? Any sense of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: My view, it's absolutely inconceivable that that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Because by the time it started happening, it was houses within the town that were being burnt, and the Bosnian Serb forces plus Greek mercenaries and others were in the town. I just -- it's inconceivable to me that there were at that stage Bosnian fighters in town setting fires to houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about in the hills?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In the hills, it's statistically possible. I'm -- the only occasion in my own experience of people leaving burning their houses was Serb population leaving Sarajevo sometime later, and houses on the hill were on fire then. So it happened. General Baxter, Colonel Baxter's report indicated that, but my view is that it unlikely and that I would have thought when the fighting was coming in, troops attacking the village, if the men were -- they would have got the hell out of there. They wouldn't have sat around and burned things and slightly adding, adding to that is the fact that the -- we first arrived in Zepa, there were -- and I think I said earlier, 50 to 80 people in the town and it was over the next few days that people started coming in. Again, here speculation, were they coming in from their houses or were they coming in from the forest? I simply don't know. And some of the earlier buildings that were on fire, we saw in the first day. But the ones within Zepa itself, I'm absolutely convinced was done by Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just this in relation to that last extract, could this be a reference to the retreating Zepa Brigade setting fire to houses as they try to disappear in the opposite direction? Would there be any strategic or tactical purpose in that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Can we just read it again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to read what the translation says, I've got it in front of me. It says, "1030 hours the setting fire of houses and marking, the line of the brigade"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes piling in by setting fire to the houses, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get that Mr. Dibb, and the helpful remark from interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: So marking the line of the brigade by setting fire to houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all if there is a foundation to be laid, and I'm frankly not sure if there is because I don't have this document here, we were just notified that they were going to use it a few minutes ago. But if there is a foundation to be laid about, first of all whose brigade we're talking about? We don't even know from my learned friend's question what we're talking about, whether we're talking about Serb forces or Bosnian forces. I think to go further on this point is just inviting more speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I have a moment? We've got nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. Now, can I have a resume of where we stand with the other Defence teams? Mr. Zivanovic, you had required -- you had requested 15 minutes. Do you still need them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours I'll not cross-examine this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Nikolic, you had requested 15 minutes. Will you be cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, you had requested ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And we inform the Court that I won't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. And Mr. Ostojic, you needed 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We've got seven minutes. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dibb, my name is John Ostojic. I represent Mr. Ljubisa Beara. Sir, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions. In particular, I just want to clarify, and maybe you could specify for me, when you were in Tuzla in July of 1995, I think you said you were there on the 14th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, I have a clear recollect -- recollection of being there on Bastille Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And were you there for until the 16th; is that correct, because I wasn't sure with your answer?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Neither am I. I think I'm pretty certain the trip to Kladanj had to be on a different day so 15, 16th, I would guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me understand your relationship with the civil affairs officer or that unit or department. Did you exchange information between various civil affairs officers such as Edward Joseph?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: He wasn't in my direct reporting line.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I realise that but --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: So likewise, I wouldn't -- I don't think, deliberately keep things from him, but I would be reporting up through Smith's office and what disseminated down wouldn't necessarily be me giving him a face-to-face direct briefing, but it was -- it was a reasonably close team within BHC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were with Mr. Joseph together in Zepa, correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just give me the dates again roughly, was it July 20th or 25th about?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again working off my previous statement, 25th to the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During that entire time, Mr. Joseph was there with you basically?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: What I don't recall is when he left, and I'm not sure if he stayed on after the last civilians left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember seeing Mr. Joseph on the 14th of July in Tuzla at all?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please pause between answer and question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your direct examination that you received information about the massacre in Srebrenica. Can you share with us from whom did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Not sure at all where we first heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who is the we? I'm only asking you, actually.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Well, we in general HQ UNPROFOR, but me personally, no, I don't remember where the first -- where the first report came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn from Mr. Joseph that as early as the 17th of July, that men, Bosnian Muslims, who were fleeing Srebrenica, arrived in Tuzla after a week long ordeal?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: It's difficult to say for certain. Again, I'm aware that people, some people, did get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And from whom did you obtain that awareness?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again, no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did you obtain it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Again not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if Mr. Joseph ever shared with you that some of the men from the Srebrenica area arrived and that the UNMOs, the civil affairs, and others have reported and described that there were 5.000 to 6.000 who crossed over to the BiH second command?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't recall that but that sort of information would have been passed out more -- it would have been passed out the morning prayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when you say morning prayers, those are your early morning briefing sessions would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For lack of a better description?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if General Smith was aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, was -- is this information that would be deemed necessary and critical for him to make any decisions relating to the actual war that was happening, that he'd be provided with that information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, the opposite of that, if he's not provided that information, it could lead to disinformation, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah, it would have made his job more difficult, more difficult to make an informed decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me with this, if you can, who is your counterpart if any, that was dealing with the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Captain Bliss.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know to what extent Captain Bliss was trying to obtain information as to the whereabouts or the status of the Bosnian men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this cable issue. When various Divisions or units were sending cables to either Sarajevo or Zagreb, would you and General Smith be routinely copied on those?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Sorry, cables originating from?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's say the civil affairs office, or the senior civil affairs officer, Ken Biser, for example?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I don't think I would necessarily have seen or -- I know I wouldn't have seen all of them, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: General Smith would have seen some, but I imagine that the volume of traffic would have been such he would not have seen them all. But I'm speculating on that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in any event the crucial thing for a general such as General Smith who is commanding this is not necessarily that he see the actual cable, but he at the very least be informed of it; would I be right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: That he be informed of?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The contents.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: The contents? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you quickly now this document, which is from the 17th of July 1995. With the Court's permission and the assistance of the usher, and we do have a number. It is 1D00374, if that could be brought up on the e-court. Just in the minute or two that we have left, may I ask just this one question or do you want to quit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long is it going to take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To ask the question, 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes go ahead and we finish there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just describe for me the cover sheet, Mr. Dibb, if you will.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Cover sheet of this, it's United Nations headed paper, appears to be a document that would have been faxed, though I don't see the fax transmission number shown on it, from Ken Biser.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who drafted it? It's right above his name, two lines?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Sorry, where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Where you read Ken Biser.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Edward Joseph, but in any event who on this list - just this last question - who on this list of individuals would have informed General Smith of the important or relevant documents contained on this most immediate and restricted outgoing fax?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS NEASON DIBB.
utterances.text: I mean what -- I'd like to read the whole thing at slower time if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it until tomorrow, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Dibb, we are adjourning. We'll have continuation of your testimony tomorrow morning. Mr. McCloskey, please make sure that the previous witness will be present tomorrow for the continuation of his testimony. Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've already made those arrangements. May I raise one very, very quick issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Court has ordered us to provide certain information concerning the remainder of the Prosecution's case. Logistically, we are still trying to contact some witnesses to give the Court the most realistic view of what the schedule is going to look like. We would ask respectfully for another day to complete that project. I've canvassed as many of my friends as I could and there is no objection to my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dibb, you're not to communicate with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony between now and when you continue and finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.
